questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with sudden onset erythema and swelling over pre-existing hypopigmented patches on his face and upper limbs. He was diagnosed with borderline tuberculoid leprosy 3 months ago and recently completed 6 months of MDT. Nerve tenderness is present. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral prednisolone 40 mg/day and continue MDT
questions.exp: This is a Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurring in borderline leprosy. Treatment is oral prednisolone starting at 40 mg/day with gradual tapering over 6 months. MDT should be continued. Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2), not Type 1 reactions.

questions.q: A 65-year-old diabetic woman presents with large, tense blisters on the trunk and flexures for 2 weeks. Nikolsky sign is negative. Biopsy shows subepidermal bullae with eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence reveals linear IgG and C3 deposition at the basement membrane zone. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense blisters, negative Nikolsky sign, subepidermal bullae with eosinophils, and linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF. First-line treatment is oral prednisolone at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day. Rituximab is reserved for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with painful erosions in her oral cavity for 3 months followed by flaccid blisters on the trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. Serology shows anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris presents with mucosal involvement, flaccid blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, suprabasal acantholysis, and IgG intercellular deposits. Initial treatment is high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1-1.5 mg/kg/day). Steroid-sparing agents like MMF or azathioprine are added for long-term control.

questions.q: A 22-year-old college student presents with multiple hypopigmented, mildly scaly patches over the chest and upper back. Under Wood's lamp, the patches show golden-yellow fluorescence. KOH mount shows short curved hyphae and clusters of spores resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor (pityriasis versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur. The pathognomonic KOH finding is 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (short hyphae and budding yeast). Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow or coppery-orange fluorescence.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless indurated ulcer on his right forearm that appeared 2 months ago after a thorn prick. Biopsy from the edge shows suppurative granulomas with Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon. Culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar at 37 degrees C shows cigar-shaped yeast cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii presents after trauma (typically thorn prick) with painless ulcer. Histopathology shows Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon. It is dimorphic: mycelial form at room temperature and cigar-shaped yeast at 37 degrees C on culture. Treatment is oral itraconazole.

questions.q: A 5-year-old immunocompetent child presents with multiple flesh-colored, umbilicated papules over the trunk and axillae. Mother reports similar lesions in his classmates. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Oral acyclovir 200 mg five times daily
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum presents with umbilicated papules caused by a poxvirus. In immunocompetent children, curettage or cryotherapy are effective first-line physical treatments. Imiquimod can be used but evidence is weaker. In HIV patients, lesions are larger, more numerous, and treatment focuses on antiretroviral therapy.

questions.q: A 58-year-old male presents with a painful vesicular eruption along the left T5 dermatome for 3 days with decreased vision and red eye. Slit-lamp examination shows dendritic ulcers on the cornea. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days plus urgent ophthalmology referral
Topical acyclovir 5% cream to skin lesions
Famciclovir 250 mg three times daily for 7 days alone
questions.exp: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) involves the V1 branch of the trigeminal nerve. Corneal involvement requires urgent ophthalmology referral and systemic antiviral therapy. Valacyclovir 1 g TDS for 7 days has superior bioavailability. Topical antivirals alone are insufficient for systemic HZO with ocular involvement.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a single painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL is non-reactive. What is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
opts: Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate from the ulcer
questions.exp: Primary syphilitic chancre is painless with indurated edges and non-tender lymphadenopathy. VDRL can be non-reactive in primary syphilis during the seronegative window period. Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate demonstrating Treponema pallidum is the gold standard diagnosis in primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 20-year-old sexually active female presents with purulent cervical and urethral discharge. Gram stain shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. She has no drug allergies. What is the current recommended treatment?
opts: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g orally single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Uncomplicated gonorrhea is treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g orally for co-treatment of possible co-existing chlamydia. Fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin are no longer recommended due to widespread resistance. Dual therapy also reduces emergence of antibiotic resistance.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with non-scarring alopecia, malar rash, oral ulcers, and joint pains for 6 months. ANA is positive at 1:640 homogeneous pattern, anti-dsDNA is elevated, and complement C3/C4 are low. Urinalysis shows proteinuria. Which cutaneous manifestation is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) lesions characterized by erythema, follicular plugging, atrophy, scarring, and dyspigmentation are the most specific cutaneous feature of lupus erythematosus. Malar rash and photosensitivity are sensitive but less specific. Only about 5-10% of DLE patients progress to SLE.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, violaceous discoloration of eyelids, and erythematous scaling papules over the interphalangeal joints of the hands. CPK is markedly elevated. Skin biopsy shows interface dermatitis with mucin deposition. The knuckle papules are pathognomonic for which diagnosis?
questions.exp: Gottron's papules are flat-topped violaceous papules over the dorsal surface of interphalangeal joints — a pathognomonic feature of dermatomyositis. The heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital discoloration) is also pathognomonic. Dermatomyositis requires screening for underlying malignancy in adults over 40.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male with plaque psoriasis involving 15% BSA has failed topical therapy and is started on methotrexate. After 3 months, he develops nausea, oral ulcers, and pancytopenia. He was also prescribed co-trimoxazole for a urinary tract infection recently. What is the mechanism of this dangerous interaction?
opts: Co-trimoxazole induces cytochrome P450 enzymes increasing methotrexate metabolism
Trimethoprim also inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, potentiating methotrexate toxicity
Sulfamethoxazole displaces methotrexate from protein binding reducing efficacy
Co-trimoxazole increases renal tubular reabsorption of methotrexate
questions.exp: Trimethoprim (in co-trimoxazole) inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, the same enzyme inhibited by methotrexate, leading to severe potentiation of methotrexate toxicity including pancytopenia and mucositis. NSAIDs also increase methotrexate toxicity by reducing renal excretion. This co-trimoxazole-methotrexate combination is contraindicated.

questions.q: A 28-year-old with severe atopic dermatitis unresponsive to topical steroids and tacrolimus is started on a biologic targeting IL-4R-alpha, blocking both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling. After 16 weeks, EASI score improves by 75%. What is this drug?
questions.exp: Dupilumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting IL-4R-alpha (IL-4 receptor alpha subunit), blocking both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling — the key Th2 cytokines in atopic dermatitis. It is FDA-approved for moderate-to-severe AD. Secukinumab targets IL-17A (psoriasis); ustekinumab targets IL-12/23; guselkumab targets IL-23.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female develops fever, targetoid lesions with dusky centers, and painful erosions of the lips and conjunctivae. Skin detachment affects approximately 35% of BSA. She was started on lamotrigine 3 weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Skin detachment greater than 30% BSA with mucosal involvement and a recent drug trigger indicates Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). Lamotrigine is a well-known cause. SJS involves less than 10% and SJS/TEN overlap is 10-30%. Management: stop the offending drug, transfer to burns unit, supportive care, consider cyclosporine or IVIG.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male repeatedly develops a well-demarcated, hyperpigmented, round plaque at the exact same site on the dorsum of his right hand each time he takes ibuprofen. On re-challenge, a new blister forms at the same site with surrounding erythema. What type of drug reaction is this?
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) recurs at identical sites with each re-exposure to the offending drug. NSAIDs are common culprits. The lesion leaves residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Histology shows interface dermatitis with numerous eosinophils and melanophages in the dermis. The pathomechanism involves resident CD8+ T-effector memory cells.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasia with a central ulcerated area on his nose. He is a fair-skinned farmer with decades of sun exposure. Biopsy confirms basal cell carcinoma. What is the treatment of choice for this high-risk facial site?
opts: Wide local excision with 1 cm margin
questions.exp: Nodular BCC on the nose (H-zone high-risk site) is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, which offers the highest cure rate (>99%) with maximal tissue sparing — critical for cosmetically sensitive facial areas. Imiquimod is only appropriate for superficial BCC. Wide 1 cm margins are excessive and disfiguring on the nose.

questions.q: A 70-year-old chronic smoker presents with a firm, erythematous papule on the lower lip that has grown to 1.5 cm over 3 months with enlarged regional lymph nodes. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which histopathological feature indicates the worst prognosis?
questions.exp: Perineural invasion in squamous cell carcinoma is a high-risk feature indicating poor prognosis, increased local recurrence, and risk of metastasis. Other poor prognostic features include poor differentiation, depth of invasion greater than 2 mm, immunosuppression, and anatomic location (ear, lip, scalp). Perineural invasion necessitates adjuvant radiation.

questions.q: A 45-year-old Caucasian male presents with an asymmetric pigmented lesion on his back, 12 mm diameter, with irregular borders and multiple colors. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, irregular streaks, and blue-white veil. Excisional biopsy is performed. What measurement primarily determines the T-stage of melanoma per current AJCC staging?
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (measured in mm from the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell) is the primary determinant of T-stage in melanoma per current AJCC 8th edition staging. Clark's level is no longer used for T-staging. Ulceration and mitotic rate also influence sub-staging. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended for Breslow thickness greater than 1 mm.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive male with CD4 count of 80 cells/uL develops multiple purplish-red nodules over the lower limbs and oral mucosa. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells with vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. LANA-1 (HHV-8 latent nuclear antigen) is positive on immunohistochemistry. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV) and is an AIDS-defining malignancy. Spindle cell proliferation with vascular spaces, RBC extravasation, and LANA-1 positivity confirm the diagnosis. Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) mimics KS clinically but shows lobular vascular proliferation with Warthin-Starry positive bacilli and responds to antibiotics.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female presents with patches of depigmentation on both hands and perioral region for 1 year. Wood's lamp shows chalk-white fluorescence with sharp margins. She has a family history of autoimmune thyroid disease. Dermoscopy shows absence of perifollicular pigmentation with leukotrichia. What does this finding predict?
opts: Poor response to topical or phototherapy treatment
Excellent response to narrowband UVB phototherapy
questions.exp: Leukotrichia (white hair within the vitiligo patch) and absence of perifollicular pigmentation on dermoscopy indicate destruction of follicular melanocyte reservoir — the source of repigmentation. This predicts poor response to topical therapies and phototherapy. Perifollicular pigmentation on dermoscopy is the most favorable prognostic sign in vitiligo.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with multiple discrete round patches of hair loss on the scalp with 'exclamation mark' hairs at the margins. No scarring is present. Dermoscopy shows yellow dots and broken hairs. What is the first-line treatment for patchy alopecia areata involving less than 25% of the scalp?
opts: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 5-10 mg/mL every 4-6 weeks
questions.exp: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (5-10 mg/mL) injected every 4-6 weeks is the first-line treatment for patchy alopecia areata with less than 50% scalp involvement. Systemic steroids are used for rapidly progressive or extensive disease. DPCP (contact immunotherapy) is reserved for extensive or steroid-unresponsive cases.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse progressive hair loss, scalp scale, and pruritus. Trichoscopy shows peripilar casts and perifollicular erythema. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrate around the infundibulum with destruction of sebaceous glands. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp
questions.exp: Lichen planopilaris (LPP) is a primary cicatricial alopecia. Characteristic features include perifollicular erythema, peripilar casts (tubular scales) on trichoscopy, and lymphocytic destruction of the infundibulum with sebaceous gland loss on biopsy. DLE also causes scarring alopecia but shows follicular plugging and interface changes with mucin. Treatment includes hydroxychloroquine.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic burrows between finger web spaces, genitalia, and axillae, worse at night. Three other family members have similar complaints. Dermoscopy shows the 'delta-wing jet with contrail' sign. What is the treatment of choice for the entire family?
opts: Topical permethrin 5% cream applied to the entire body overnight, repeated after 7 days
questions.exp: Topical permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies, applied from neck downward for 8-12 hours and repeated after 7 days. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously. Lindane is neurotoxic and contraindicated in children under 2 years and pregnant women. Oral ivermectin is preferred for crusted scabies or large institutional outbreaks.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient from Rajasthan presents with a painless ulcer on his face with indurated, violaceous, undermined edges and satellite lesions developing over 4 months after an insect bite. Slit-skin smear from the edge shows amastigotes within macrophages. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Sodium stibogluconate (SSG) 20 mg/kg/day IM for 28 days
questions.exp: Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania tropica presents with painless ulcer with undermined edges. Diagnosis is by slit-skin smear showing Leishman-Donovan bodies (amastigotes in macrophages). First-line treatment is sodium stibogluconate (SSG) 20 mg/kg/day IM for 28 days. Miltefosine is an oral alternative primarily for visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.q: A lepromatous leprosy patient on MDT develops tender, erythematous nodules all over the body, fever, arthralgia, and iridocyclitis. Slit-skin smear shows numerous acid-fast bacilli. What is the immediate treatment?
opts: Add thalidomide 100-300 mg/day or prednisolone and continue MDT
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction in LL/BL leprosy. Treatment: thalidomide (100-300 mg/day, drug of choice in males and non-childbearing females) or prednisolone for acute ENL. MDT must be continued throughout all lepra reactions. Clofazimine 300 mg/day is added for recurrent or steroid-dependent ENL.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with psoriatic arthritis uncontrolled on methotrexate is prescribed a TNF-alpha inhibitor. Two months after starting treatment, he develops a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. What mandatory pre-treatment screening should have been done?
opts: Serum uric acid and urine analysis
QuantiFERON-TB Gold or Mantoux test plus chest X-ray
Hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-HCV alone
questions.exp: Before starting any TNF-alpha inhibitor, mandatory screening for latent tuberculosis (QuantiFERON-TB Gold or Mantoux/TST) and chest X-ray must be performed. Positive LTBI requires prophylactic isoniazid for at least 1 month before starting the biologic. Hepatitis B screening is also required. Failure to screen can lead to reactivation TB.

questions.q: A 16-year-old female presents with open and closed comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodular acne on the face, chest, and back. She also has irregular menstrual cycles and hirsutism. She has not responded to doxycycline and adapalene for 6 months. Which systemic drug is most appropriate considering her hormonal profile?
opts: Combined oral contraceptive pill with anti-androgenic progestin
Oral azithromycin 500 mg three times per week
questions.exp: This patient has hormonal acne with clinical signs of androgen excess (irregular cycles, hirsutism), suggesting PCOS. Combined oral contraceptives with anti-androgenic progestins (cyproterone acetate, drospirenone) or spironolactone are appropriate. Hormonal evaluation and treatment should be prioritized. Isotretinoin is considered but hormonal control of androgen excess is more targeted here.

questions.q: A 28-year-old fair-skinned male presents with persistent central facial erythema, flushing triggered by hot beverages, telangiectasia, and occasional inflammatory papules but no comedones. Which combination best addresses both the erythema and papules?
opts: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus topical fluorinated steroid
Topical metronidazole or azelaic acid for papules plus topical brimonidine for persistent erythema
questions.exp: Rosacea is characterized by central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, and inflammatory papules without comedones. Topical metronidazole and azelaic acid address the inflammatory component. Topical brimonidine (alpha-2 agonist) or oxymetazoline reduces persistent erythema by vasoconstriction. Topical fluorinated steroids are contraindicated as they worsen rosacea.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with plaque psoriasis undergoes PUVA therapy with oral 8-methoxypsoralen (8-MOP). After completing 150 sessions over 3 years, the dermatologist counsels him about the most important long-term risk. What is it?
opts: Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma
questions.exp: The most important dose-limiting long-term toxicity of PUVA therapy is increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma (dose-dependent) and, with higher cumulative doses, melanoma. Photoaging and PUVA lentigines also occur. Patients are advised to use UV-protective eyewear for 24 hours after psoralen intake to prevent lens damage. Regular skin cancer surveillance is essential.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive tightening of the skin over the fingers and face for 2 years with difficulty swallowing. On examination she has sclerodactyly, calcinosis, telangiectasia, and Raynaud's phenomenon. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. Which esophageal abnormality is most expected?
opts: Hypomotility of the lower two-thirds of the esophagus due to smooth muscle fibrosis
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (limited systemic sclerosis) — Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia — is associated with anti-centromere antibody. Fibrosis of the smooth muscle in the lower two-thirds of the esophagus causes hypomotility, dysphagia, and gastroesophageal reflux. This is the characteristic visceral manifestation of limited SSc.
